This research focuses on a change to the usual FGMRES method by using a change to the norm in a non-standard way. We analyze how this change can lead to better solutions numerically, particularly when dealing with large and cumbersome matrices common today. Our approach involves a simple way to make this change that can be easily handled computationally, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness with implicit Einstein gravity solvers.

The accuracy of registering dynamic, noise-affected organs to preoperative models using only 3D surface data is crucial for enhancing surgical safety. A novel approach has been developed to identify and reduce noisy endoscopic data by analyzing its scale in relation to the organ's deformation, with the goal of registering the organ to an anatomical reference. A method has been proposed to detect the level of noise in endoscopic data by examining its characteristics, and a new variational regularisation function has been developed to guide organ reconstruction. The effectiveness of this technique has been demonstrated through tests on synthetic data and comparison with existing organ reconstruction models.

This work introduces a novel end-to-end learning framework for free-form object displacements and rotations, aiming to handle complex scenarios involving occlusions, objects with varying depths, and interactions. A complex dataset is employed, subjecting the network to occlusions, object interactions, and generative masking challenges. Furthermore, a new dataset is created to evaluate the model's performance on real-world cases, object displacements, rotations, and mask prediction. However, results show difficulties in handling occlusions and complex interactions, and difficulties in accurately estimating masks for real-world scenes.

Deep neural networks excel at pattern recognition but consume significant power due to multiplications in their inference process. We propose a novel neural network - a ResNet based reservoir with auxiliary skip connections and a dense classifier - that uses a simplified matrix multiplication for inference, thus eliminating multiplications. This approach enables low-power inference with embedded systems. Our proposed network maintains a residual structure, comprising two auxiliary skip connections, a fully connected decoder, and a ResNet-based classifier, also replicating the pre-network feature transformation. Evaluating our approach on MNIST and CIFAR-10 shows a notable finding - simple complex, but efficient networks can achieve a performance nearly identical to well-honed ANNs with five times less power consumption, just one hundred times more neurons, and nearly four times the memory footprint.

This research investigates the impact of strong magnetic fields on the properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter, focusing on a modified Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model that incorporates linear sigma fields. Calculations were carried out in the presence of strong magnetic fields using the functional determinant method and the grand canonical partition function, with hadrons described by the relativistic Breit-Wigner mass spectrum. The equation of state under two- flavor QCD phase was determined and used to model the structure of magnetar stars. Findings suggest that the mass-radius relations of these stars align with recent X-ray observations, indicating that spin polarization in strong magnetic fields affects the quark equation of state but has negligible effect on magnetar star radius and mass relations.

A cubic graph is even-2-factorable if and only if it can be decomposed into two distinct spanning subgraphs, each consisting of a collection of even cycles. In 1967, J.A. Seressey asserted that every cubic graph can be E2F, but A.J. Schwenk in 1974 disproved this claim by providing a method to construct non-E2F cubic graphs from those that are non-planar. This study presents an algorithm to identify non-E2F cubic graphs and expands the initial set of non-E2F graphs proposed by Schwenk.

Our new tool, Timeloops, is a precise time-based system call filter for Linux
containers that allows applications to function within specified time limits.
Although system call filtering is a valuable technique for security, virtualization, and content delivery, it poses significant programming challenges,
particularly for interpreted languages like PHP and Python. To overcome this barrier, Timeloops leverages Python and PHP extensions,
enabling transparent operation for existing applications. The filter's complexity is managed through straightforward configuration,
specifying the maximum time, system call name, and the corresponding time it should take. We have evaluated Timeloops for its capacity to specify
application timeframes for system calls, demonstrating that it can successfully deliver applications that are 2 orders of magnitude slower than they should be,
while accurately matching them presents a greater challenge. Furthermore, Timeloops demonstrates that system call filtering can be effectively applied to
production-ready applications written in PHP and Python.

In practical scenarios where detection is incomplete, accurately identifying and tracking targets that are not directly observed becomes a significant challenge, particularly when working with systems that have restricted fields of view. In developing cooperative strategies for multiple agents tasked with tracking multiple undetected targets, reducing computational complexity is essential, especially when working with limited fields of view. The proposed method achieves a substantial improvement in computational efficiency for single-agent systems, and when extended to multi-agent setups with specific constraints, it results in a notable reduction in computational complexity that grows exponentially with the number of agents, offering a more scalable solution. Additionally, the approach incorporates a cost function designed to minimize the total search time across all agents, thereby optimizing tracking performance. By evaluating a Monte Carlo simulation, the study demonstrates effective tracking of multiple targets through coordinated agent movements, even when detections are partially obtained, and provides an accurate estimate of localization errors resulting from the absence of feedback from successful detections.

This research aims to apply the concept of observability inequality as a tool for achieving population extinction within a specific reaction-diffusion model. The specific approach involves choosing a control mechanism that is constrained by certain bounds, then demonstrating that it's possible to extinguish the population in a defined, final time period, provided this period is sufficiently long.

In the Penalty Shootout version of football, a team is awarded three points if they convert two out of five penalties, making this format an ideal setting to evaluate the efficiency of artificial intelligence. In our study, we assess the performance of the D4P policy, which uses deep reinforcement learning, across various challenging situations to demonstrate its potential for improving policy representation in tasks with limited experience opportunities. Our results show that the D4P policy outperforms a conventional deep neural network-based baseline, a difference that is significant at the 0.01 level, indicating the benefits of product of expert approaches even when evaluating a single expert system. Moreover, we found interesting patterns in the penalty points distribution between the two policies, revealing unusual actions—such as penalizing opponents or losing possession of the ball—yielding the same reward as taking a shot at the goal, indicating the AI's difficulty in learning generalizable policies from limited data.

A common full waveform inversion method involves aligning simulated and observed wavefields in time and space after applying non-linear transformations. However, utilizing time-domain wavefields directly can lead to unrealistic high-frequency components and violations of physics during the optimization process. As a result, many researchers prefer to match phase velocities only. A full waveform inversion using cross-correlation matches phase velocities but can be sensitive to misalignments in frequency or time due to premature convergence towards minimum misfit with incorrect models. In this paper, we demonstrate that incorporating a combination of cross-correlation and aligned phase velocities can be achieved through convex optimization without introducing local minima or non-convex alignment terms in the cost function. We also show the effectiveness of this approach through 2D synthetic tests.

We investigate the interaction between two species competing for space in an asymmetric noisy voter model, where one species has the capability to convert areas occupied by the other species, but not vice versa, all set within a noisy environment that enables spontaneous changes of species placement. Our research reveals that the competition leads to several outcomes, including the elimination of one species, the coexistence of both species, or the formation of domains controlled by the more aggressive species, all dependent on the specific conditions of the environment and the level of noise present.

A novel two-phase protocol, TFIET (Two-Phase Information and Energy Transfer), is proposed for simultaneous data and power delivery to devices during wireless communication. In the first phase, some time is dedicated to transmitting useful information to the device, while the remaining time is used for supplying energy from a powerful base station to a weaker one through a relay. During the second phase, the device leverages acquired energy to send data back to the base station via a relay. The primary objective is to maximize the sum of throughputs for both uplink and downlink transmissions by carefully controlling the relay's behavior. The main constraints considered are dedicated time allocation, relay's beamforming, and sufficient energy availability for the device. The problem becomes non-convex due to a constraint involving a non-concave function, but it can be resolved via an iterative method. Numerical results show that TFIET outperforms a scheme where data delivery is purely energy-based.

Recent telework necessities have accelerated the need for automating laboratory arrangements, particularly interactive experimental systems with several human and robotic participants. Utilizing modern high-speed broadband networks, these setups now allow for remote collaboration among people and automated devices. Although automated and remote-controlled systems with multiple agents have been around for some time, the latest advancements in technology have led to new possibilities for their implementation. Utilizing a generalizable, modular software architecture for these systems has been shown to be beneficial. This approach allows the systems to be easily adapted to new tasks while keeping the complex parts of the set-up away from the controlling scripts. A study was also conducted on the impact of increased latency and bandwidth limitations on a systems that previously operated with people present but were now controlled from a distance. With the aid of wide-area networks, this study was conducted by connecting the systems to the laboratories of the researchers over distances of 100 meters to 500 kilometers. The results of the experiment were published in a paper at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation.

The influence of electrostatic phase plates on the size and current density of electron probes is a well-studied topic, with various designs proposed over the past few decades. The impact of key parameters, such as fill-factor, feeding method, and pixel arrangement on a simulation model, is examined in this research to support future phase plate designs for scanning electron microscopes. Utilizing a 2D finite element method (FEM) to simulate electron probes, we analyze how these parameters affect electron optical performance. Results reveal that high fill-factor plates yield the smallest electron probe size but the lowest current density, whereas low fill-factor plates produce a larger electron probe size but higher current density. Also, certain pixel arrangements yield better current density than others at the same fill-factor. These findings are intended to provide guidance for designing electron optical phase plates for SEM applications.

We studied a specific ordinary differential equation that includes an anharmonic oscillator and a nonlocal term represented by a ratio of integrals. Our main finding is that for any given nonlinearity parameter, soliton solutions that maintain their position in space can be expressed as combinations of exponential functions of individual momentum values. A significant aspect is that given initial conditions, the oscillator's deviation from equilibrium decays at a rate determined by the larger of the two momentum values, demonstrating the interplay between nonlocal and nonlinear terms in a localized context. Also, the equation of motion can be transformed from its time-dependent form to a conservative, time-independent manner. Furthermore, we showed that adding a local, harmonic term to the equation could cause soliton solutions to behave unpredictably, whereas introducing an anharmonic oscillator term in one-dimensional systems led to solutions that could be explicitly represented as ratios of linear combinations of exponentials of individual momentum values, even with the most nonlinear scenarios. Ultimately, we discovered that soliton solutions in one dimension could be expressed as ratios of linear combinations of exponentials of individual momentum values, whereas in two or three dimensions, they cannot be represented analytically.

In this article, we investigate the Galois additive module structure in a wide range of deeply ramified finite non-abelian extensions of the rational numbers. By conducting highly precise computer experiments on the Galois additive module structure in $K|k$, where $k$ is a highly ramified local field and $K$ is its extensive non-abelian extension, a theoretical framework has been established and demonstrated through computer-generated data in a specific case study utilizing Magma software.

In searches for neutral long-lived particles, the technique employed for identification varies greatly depending on the particle's decay length, posing challenges in combining results from multiple studies utilizing different methods. At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), missing energy and particles can result from new physics, often associated with a new stable particle that cannot be easily detected due to lack of charge, necessitating focused searches for specific signatures. A proposed approach, a unified model, combines a visible neutral long-lived particle with missing energy or particles under the assumption of a two-step particle decay. The visible component's characteristics and the associated missing energy or particle data can help determine the properties of an hypothetical neutral long-lived particle. To evaluate this, simulations were conducted for supersymmetric models featuring a neutral stau as the lightest supersymmetric particle, demonstrating how visible component ratios influence interpretations and strategies, particularly when predicting search outcomes based on properties such as proper decay length.

This paper investigates the diachronic development of the contextual variability measure (CV) in language through an examination of the factors influencing its changes. Researchers analyzed modifications in the relationship between words and their contexts over time, using 1150 American English Wikipedia articles from the year 2019 as corpus data. The study specifically focused on seven words that exhibit a significant change in variability and explored the effects of document diversity on contextual changes using multivariate analysis. The findings revealed the impact of registration content on the variability of word contexts, as well as the influence of context density and complexity on context representations. Furthermore, the study found variations in the changes that affect less common words in less complex contexts. The paper also discusses the implications of the results for contextual models in NLP and proposes new, more appropriate metrics for measuring semantic changes in language.

A novel approach is proposed to detect a hypothetical particle, known as the axion, by examining the fluctuations in the Sun's light output. Any absorption caused by an ultra-faint particle in a few solar photons would result in a measurable effect on the Space Power Spectrum, far exceeding that predicted by cosmic variance and the effects of Earth's rotation and orbit. If the axion's cutoff wavelength is longer than a few micrometers, it depletes dark matter in the universe, as the axion's field would reach its critical value within the age of the cosmos. Consequently, dark matter in the universe would have to be composed of massive, clumped particles rather than this specific type of axion, as a few solar photons would not be the only place where this axion could exist.

During retinogenesis, the inner retinal layers are formed through the migration of post-mitotic neurons from the neural retina's surface to its interior. The distribution of these neurons is non-random, yet the underlying principles governing their placement during migration remain unknown. Utilizing high-resolution confocal time-lapse images, the spatial coordinates of live nuclei were tracked in 3D space and time within the developing mouse retina. The resulting dataset provides the first detailed map of migration dynamics in the inner retina, revealing the speed of moving nuclei, their direction of movement, and the distances covered during a defined time period. The data also shows the angles of movement in relation to the retina's surface, the frequencies of moving and stationary nuclei, the shapes of their trajectories, and the distribution of their locations within the retinal layers. The elaborate patterns of motion and position were characterized, including the effects of layer boundaries on their behavior, the distribution of nuclei in the different retinal layers, the distances between the layers, the distances from the retina's surface, the angles of their movement in relation to the surface, the frequencies of nuclei in the different layers, and the lengths they travel during a defined time period. The data generated from this study will serve as a standard for assessing perturbations caused by genetic modifications or the inhibition of signaling pathways and the expression of specific proteins during migration.

This study explores the use of sparse sampling combined with sparse representations for recovering sparse images from incomplete data, a common challenge in applications like compressed sensing. Initially, the study leverages the fact that most image spectra are concentrated in a limited range to construct an optimal phase-encoding gradient matrix that minimizes mutual coherence with the sparse sampling matrix. Although minimizing mutual coherence theoretically guarantees robust reconstruction performance with an optimized coherence factor, minimizing it directly can lead to computation issues and potentially counterproductive results in practical applications. Consequently, the study introduces two novel optimization objectives, combining the optimized coherence factor with actual reconstruction errors. These new objectives balance the minimization of mutual coherence in the sensing matrix with the maintainability of reconstruction errors within an acceptable range. To achieve this, the study employs a novel two-stage gradient design to generate a sensing matrix that ensures a well-distributed and recoverable phase-encoding gradient matrix with a well-behaved optimization landscape. Furthermore, a new optimization algorithm, termed Two-Stage Adaptive Descent (TAD), is developed to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem effectively. Finally, the study validates the efficacy and generality of the proposed method through various numerical experiments and visual comparisons on real image data sets.

We investigate various active system models in different dimensions from 2 to 5, simating their behavior over time spacings of up to $10^5$. The goal is to identify how these systems respond in different dimensional environments by analyzing their dynamic properties. Our study involves multiple models, including those that reproduce the fish velocity distribution, and we examine their hydrodynamic, non-equilibrium, dynamics. The results show that the systems' behavior in different dimensions can be categorized into three distinct regimes: linearized hydrodynamics, a intermediate range, and equilibrium in the highest dimension. The most striking aspect is the robust universal scaling observed in the second regime, which defies the predictions of traditional hydrodynamic theories and equates data across the different dimensions studied. This discovery is further supported by comparing the precise scaling parameters of our simulations with those estimated from biological observations.

The accuracy of text extraction from ID cards is heavily dependent on the quality of the data used, and since NLP systems are now being widely applied, ensuring high-quality NLP training datasets is crucial. This study devises a new category of extraction errors, called ambiguous labels, and conducts a detailed analysis to develop a guideline for correctly identifying them. A novel sampling strategy is also presented, and its effectiveness is compared through multiple experiments using both human annotators and an existing text classification model, demonstrating the utility of this strategy in producing high-quality, well-annotated data.

In this paper, we examine the behavior of a driven quantum system under constant force, using a model where the Hamiltonian changes periodically in time. We explore how these driven systems respond to various drive frequencies and initial conditions, specifically comparing the performance of driven and undriven cases. Our research involves investigating the decay of wave packets in both scenarios, and we find that the driven system exhibits a characteristic decay pattern that can be used to understand the properties of the system. We also discuss the connection between our results and previous research on the quantum Hall effect and other related topics.

A study of nine detected exoplanets/small asteroids in six systems revealed that their velocities do not match the expected range for independent asteroids. Instead, data indicated a significant acceleration in the same direction as their planet's rotation for five of the detected cases. If authentic, this exoplanet swarm is held against the planet by its own gravitational pull rather than just the planet's attraction, implying a minimum mass of 1.3% of the host planet's mass. If exoplanets/asteroids are typical of detected transits, a significant fraction of potential false-positive observations may be due to planets with their own exoplanet swarms.

Let X be a compact surface and G be the group of homeomorphisms of X. If a subgroup H of G acts transitively on the interior of X, we determine the conditions under which H is considered precompact, specifically when H is finite or when X is non-Euclidean and H is itself precompact. Furthermore, when X is the Euclidean surface, we identify the scenario where H must be finite if it acts transitively and is precompact.

We can determine the preimage of a continuity point under a rational map from R^n to R^m at that point, given the coordinates of its image, for both two and higher dimensions, using a linear-bounded automaton. This preimage decision problem can't be solved with a smaller complexity class than LFNP. Moreover, when it comes to all points of continuity, our previous findings and those of others show that determining whether a rational function is entirely continuous lies within a specific subset of the third level of the W-hierarchy, but not necessarily any lower part of this hierarchy. Consequently, the set of entirely continuous rational functions constitutes a core component of this third level of the W-hierarchy.

A major limitation of reservoir computing is its applicability to dynamic systems that exhibit different time scales and multiple co-existing dynamic behaviors. We investigate a complex system, the Lorenz-96 model, in its most chaotic state with infinite, disjoint attractors and various time scales, to determine if a previously unseen dynamic state can be identified using reservoir computing. By developing a preserver network that outperforms a traditional linear reservoir, we successfully map a previously unexplored region of the Lorenz-96 model's parameter space. Our findings reveal that this reservoir is capable of detecting a new co-existing state, characterized by two rotating Lorenz bars, and accurately replicates this state's distinct pattern. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this reservoir can track a time-varying model, in which the rotation period gradually decreases, and accurately capture the corresponding change in parameters. Overall, our research establishes that complex systems with multiple co-existing states and different time scales can be effectively modeled and analyzed using reservoir computing.

Feedback control relies on an initial understanding of a system's state, which informs the selection of actions to achieve the desired outcome. Determining the set of possible states that can be achieved through feedback control is thus essential. This paper presents an approach to compute the reachable state sets under specified constraints, for systems with continuous states and discrete states, in relation to dynamics that depend on the state. We demonstrate how feedback can be utilized in the computation of these reachable state sets within a designated time frame. Moreover, we provide an algorithm to calculate the corresponding set of possible states. Specifically, for systems without uncertainties or states that cannot be directly observed, the computed sets are shown to be suitable for the specification and guarantee of temporal properties.

People's beliefs about the world are influenced by their understanding of what is alive and artificial versus natural. Prior studies suggest that objects that are either alive or artificial are more easily categorized visually than natural objects, yet the extent to which these effects are separate remains unclear. This research investigated whether the ease with which objects can be visually categorized is influenced by both their perceived aliveness/artificiality and agency, or if these effects are completely independent. Participants rated objects on visual categorizability, agency, and dimensions of the animacy continuum while presenting visual categorizability as the dependent variable in both hierarchical linear models and structural equation modeling. The results indicated that visual categorizability and agency effects were entirely independent, neither of which was directly connected to the animacy continuum. Rather, both were mediated by the dimensions of the animacy continuum, demonstrating that visual categorizability and agency effects are distinctly linked to the continuum's dimensions but are not directly connected to each other or the outward appearance of objects.

Given an algebraic number zero, there is a non-zero probability that the corresponding automorphic L-function will have a zero close to the one originally given, within a specific power of its complexity. This finding contrasts with a conjecture by Barak, Goldstein, and Zauderkis which posits that the closure of such zeros is highly influential, either in explaining why certain zero patterns occur or why a 'large sieve' effect exists for occurrences within a specific range. In the process of proving this result, we develop an innovative approach, which in turn reveals the existence of a 'small sieve' effect in the case of GL(n) for n greater than 1, an observation previously unreported.

Quantitative input/output relationships in quantum systems can be effectively modeled using probed supernorms, which were developed to address issues with earlier methods. Establishing bounds on these metrics facilitates efficient approximation of quantum algorithms' behaviors. In this context, our work extends quantum relational Hoare logic to capture a wide array of input/output relations, including equitable equivalence between quantum states, equitable bipartite relations, and stochastic relations. We demonstrate that this logic can establish equitable equivalence and stochastic relations with a polynomial number of queries to the circuit, as well as establish quantitative versions of these relations without risking an exponential increase in query count compared to direct comparison or unitary transformation. Furthermore, when comparing two circuits with $n$ qubits and depth $d$, our approach ensures a probed supernorm of equivalent states is not exceeded with a probability of at least $1 - 2^{-n}$, and similarly for our quantitative logic.

In recent studies involving enclosed environments such as boats, buses, and ships, researchers observed a unique super-spreading phenomenon where most infected individuals transmitted the virus to one or few people, but in some instances, infection rates as high as 100% with transmission to ten or more individuals were observed. To understand this behavior, an SI-SI network model was developed that accounts for super-spreading events within limited time frames. This model was refined by incorporating the dynamics of an enclosed environment where infection rates and recovery rates fluctuate over time. When analyzed using stochastic simulations and deterministic models, it was discovered that short-term infections in these environments are characterized by super-spreading events and cannot be represented by standard epidemiological models. Furthermore, it was observed that the number of infected individuals reaches a peak quickly in the early stages, after which the infection levels decline and ultimately disappear. The duration of the infection within the environment was also found to be affected by the presence of an infected individual, leading to variations in infection patterns that require consideration when interpreting data.

This article begins by defining a new property, known as codiskcyclicity, which serves as a broader category than codyclicity and codiskcyclicity at a particular point. It then delves into the examination of codiskcyclicity specifically related to the interior of the unit disk. Various techniques for analyzing first and higher order differential operators are applied to investigate codiskcyclicity. It is demonstrated that both first and higher order differential operators, with certain types of coefficient behavior, generate codiskcyclic semigroups of operators. Additionally, it is shown that the codiskcyclicity at the origin is possessed by rotation semigroups of operators defined on spaces containing $l^{\infty}$.

Accurate evaluation of magnetic field strength distribution is vital for comprehension of physical dynamics in the solar atmosphere, yet vector magnetic field maps often contain significant measurement errors due to incomplete magnetic fill fraction and polarization saturation effects. This research incorporates two corrections to a typical Spitzer approximation for electron free path density current: polarization saturation and magnetic field estimation corrections. A newly modified statistical method is developed and validation shows a significant reduction in non-physical solutions compared to the original method. This custom data processing sequence is then applied to solar granulation models to demonstrate the improvement in physical solution consistency when considering partial coverage of the magnetic field. The new approach also indicates the necessary magnetic field strengths for the onset of umbral penetration.

A common challenge in Monte Carlo simulations involves a suboptimal estimation of the integrand's domain due to the nature of the method. This project proposes a novel and efficient variance reduction technique by modifying the standard normal distribution used in these simulations, specifically by adapting complex-valued affine coupling layers. When applied to simple one-dimensional cases, this method outperforms traditional variance reduction techniques, and when tested on the widely recognized Fireball model for estimating the quark-gluon plasma duration, it significantly improves upon the current estimates, potentially shifting the predicted duration by up to an order of magnitude.

Given a shift topological dynamical system (X, σ) and a recognizable morphism φ from the free group, the topological entropy of the image subshift (Y, σ) = (X, σ)^̄ can be bounded using the topological entropy of (X, σ^nd), where σ^nd denotes the natural shift map. This relationship is expressed as h(Y) ≤ ε((X, σ^nd)) * h(X, σ^nd), where the constant topological entropy h(Y) ≤ ε((X, σ^nd)) * h(X, σ^nd) depends only on the free group. This result has no analog in the context of formal language theory, where the topological entropy of (X, σ^nd) plays a significant role.

Utilizing pre-trained language models for unsupervised tasks like word sense disambiguation and named entity recognition has seen little advancement. A key limitation is the inability to leverage multiple senses or entities for one another, as is often the case in representations that map inputs to inputs. In this study, we introduce a technique called ReCross, a form of alternating attention that switches between input-to-input and input-to-input transformations, as well as one that changes the number of entities or senses per word. We applied this method to WSD and NER using both multi-sense and multi-entity inputs, and found that allowing the number of senses or entities per word to vary leads to significant performance gains, particularly for under-represented senses and entities. Our results show that ReCross outperforms the original model by a margin, as well as setting new state-of-the-art benchmarks for unsupervised WSD and NER.

This paper introduces a novel, end-to-end differentiable grid search method to efficiently determine hyperparameters for a client in a federated learning setup. It addresses a key limitation of standard grid search, which cannot be used for hyperparameter optimization when dealing with private data sets that are not openly accessible. Instead, our method creates a small,可交换数据集 through a non凸 minimization problem formed from the training data and loss functions associated with various hyperparameter combinations. Once this minimum is reached, the corresponding hyperparameter combination that results in the smallest loss function value is identified. Furthermore, our grid search approach allows for the relaxation of certain constraints, enabling a broader range of hyperparameter optimization challenges to be addressed. Experimental evidence from a decision tree training process under federated learning conditions, as well as general optimization tests, demonstrates our method's feasibility and HPO performance that is comparable to traditional grid search techniques.

The concept of a spherical Coxeter group involves a Coxeter group where a specific wedge of spheres exists, with a group element at the center of the wedge and rays extending to its conjugacy class. The number of spheres in this wedge is determined by a Coxeter group variant at a particular size. A notable result from 1990 established that a specific wedge is sufficient to define the spherical type of a non-trivial Coxeter group. However, this wedge may not always be the most efficient option. This research enhances the wedge from the Liouville and Michel research, and determines the most efficient wedge for each conjugacy class in a specified set of Coxeter group variants. These include finite Coxeter groups, affine Coxeter groups, and certain finitely generated Coxeter group variants known as G-compact, including those from a specific set of four categories.

Researchers examined a group of 14 F-type stars with unusual characteristics,
which have been identified as part of a population with distinct chemical
compositions, by assessing the elemental abundances of 18 different components,
ranging from lithium to uranium. By utilizing high-resolution, comprehensive
spectral analysis techniques, the study determined the robustness of the derived
abundances by calculating their uncertainties and evaluating the influence of
assumptions related to these stars' ages, distances, and fundamental properties
on the results. Since these stars are located in regions with low stellar
crowding, they are considered ideal for observing elements as heavy as uranium
through spectroscopy. Furthermore, the study's depth and precision in analyzing
abundances contribute significantly to advancing our understanding of chemically
distinctive stars and stellar populations, as well as the formation processes
of low-metallicity stars.

This paper utilizes a dynamic attenuated gravitational model of rumor spreading, combined with a Simulated Annealing optimization method, to analyze the information degradation of subway exit locations from the 2013 Hebei Express station incident. The study demonstrates that certain precursor elements, such as the attenuation rate and peak volume of online rumors, are deeply interconnected with ground information and can be integrated into future modeling efforts. A novel approach is also presented to decompose the data of search index fluctuations into endogenous and exogenous components, allowing the attenuation rate to be measured more accurately. The study's findings indicate that the attenuation rate can be influenced by various factors, including public sentiment, media coverage, and ground information release, and are largely consistent with actual observations.

We have examined the physical and spectral characteristics of the 1442 members of the Fornax dwarf spheroidal galaxy detected by a single-pass MACHO survey, with spectral data for a subset of these members available to constrain their physical parameters. Based on the nebular classification for 94 PNe within the cluster, the distances to Fornax were calculated using the PALF and resulted in $\bar{r}=19.6^{+1.0}_{-3.0}$ pc, which is consistent with the previously established value of $\sim$20 pc from other sources. Additionally, the PN-LPF within the Fornax cluster appears uniform, although there is a possible slight excess of dimmer entries that require verification with higher-resolution imaging. The expanded speed sound within the cluster yielded an older age estimate of $\sim$1.6 gigayear, compared to the typical normal disk age of $\sim$0.6 gigayear. The fundamental speed sound within the cluster also yields an offset of $\sim$0.6 gigayear from the normal disk value. PN outflows within the cluster are mostly low-density and slow-moving, which is in contrast to the high-density and fast-moving PN outflows typically seen in the normal disk. The PN phase within the cluster also has an older age of $\sim$10 gigayear, which is in contrast to the typical normal disk age of $\sim$0.6 gigayear.

Using vast, continuously flowing data from multiple systems is becoming increasingly commonplace. Effectively combining such data with streamlined code in Python, Java, or C++ for code maintenance and development purposes poses substantial performance hurdles when dealing with real-world datasets. We present LifeStream, an innovative code tool built on top of Apache Pulsar that enables efficient execution of numerical code and N-dimensional array operations for array types associated with scalar values or matrices, even when working with data stored in real-time. Our code stream optimizes array operations by employing in-place computations and bypassing interim data storage. In experiments conducted on diverse, real-world datasets ranging from machine learning models to simulation code, LifeStream exhibits comparable performance to state-of-the-art hand-optimized solutions, while simultaneously simplifying the development process by nearly a factor of ten in terms of coding effort.

This research paper explores the concept of Bertrand curves within the context of bi-Eulerian space-2, specifically demonstrating that these curves in these types of spaces are isospectral. A key aspect involves deriving a relationship between the coefficients of curvature in Bi-Eulerian space-2.

Software testing can be slow due to the inclusion of multiple, often redundant test cases that use different input data and check for the same type of incorrect behavior. Research suggests using machine learning to reduce the number of tests while maintaining the same level of error detection. What hinders progress in this area is that certain metrics used to evaluate efficiency are incomparable and some functions underestimate risks more than others. We compare six different metrics that can be applied to software testing using a dataset of 13,000 exercises from a popular online coding platform. We find that even simple metrics can be as effective as more complex ones and that some may be unfairly penalizing. We also discover that some performance issues are caused by an over-representation of easy-to-solve problems in the data set.

This research paper aims to develop a sophisticated model for capturing both heat changes and structural transformations that occur when a polymer experiences induced crystallization while under stress. We based our model on an innovative, temperature-sensitive structural variable and a corresponding structural second gradient, as well as a composite free energy density that reflects the material's partially crystalline nature. The resulting thermomechanical control equations include the evolution of structural variables, the first and second laws of thermomechanics, and the balance of momentum and energy. We then explored the possibility of inducing complete crystallization in an one-dimensional setting, considering both isothermal and adiabatic conditions. The problem was formulated as a minimization task for a composite functional that incorporated the variable's free energy density, the heat generated during the phase transition, and the mechanical stress balance. We successfully found the optimal temperature to induce full crystallization in a given initial configuration, and identified the precise conditions where the crystalline structure would remain stable.

Recent measurements of magnetic susceptibility in strongly soccer-ball-shaped superconducting materials exhibit a striking sensitivity to the topology of their Fermi surfaces through a scalar, periodic oscillation. This pattern's period, topological charge, and susceptibility with closed or partially open Fermi surfaces are shown to be directly influenced by the topology of their Fermi surfaces, affecting only d-wave superconducting/scalar channels. A generalizable framework is crafted to describe the topological Scotogenic Susceptibility, leveraging the Periodic Schr\"{o}dinger Scalar, and demonstrating its equivalence to a PTC/STC, while providing a concrete integral formula for its calculation.

This research compares error rate performance of coherent and conventional differential detection methods in the context of CPM signals, specifically GMSK modulation, under low signal-to-noise conditions. It involves a detailed analysis of differential detection decision rules, followed by numerical evaluation of error rates using numerical integration and Monte Carlo simulations. The study also incorporates the use of a series expansion to approximate error rates and a novel conventional differential detector based on non-linear filtering and vector quantization. The proposed detector's performance is assessed through computed error rates and simulated performance metrics, demonstrating a outperformance over the conventional method with significant improvement in error rate, up to two orders of magnitude.

It has been demonstrated that the mathematical inconsistency commonly ascribed to the grand canonical ensemble specifically applies to systems with significant constant-pressure compressibility. Furthermore, the ensemble is found to yield precise results for less compressible systems. A more comprehensive, less compressible-encompassing ensemble has been introduced. The ensemble's applicability and the understandability of certain thermodynamic phenomena previously exclusive to the grand canonical ensemble's domain have been demonstrated.

In natural language processing, mastering commonsense knowledge is crucial. However, current AI models' ability to handle this knowledge remains limited. Our research focuses on enhancing the representation of this knowledge by incorporating its inherent hierarchy. We designed a model called HIPT, which uses hierarchical classification networks to process structured, categorized knowledge in the form of statements. Our model successfully utilizes hierarchical relationships and progressive probability estimation. Testing shows HIPT outperforms other methods that handle categorized knowledge and common sense representations, particularly when models are trained with limited data through fine-tuning. Our findings indicate that neural networks benefit from learning hierarchical patterns, and thus, HIPT provides a flexible framework for exploiting various forms of structured knowledge.

The effectiveness of end-to-end automated speech recognition using RNNs has been hindered by the difficulty in modeling complex language information due to unexplored audio-text interactions. Building on previous research that utilized attention mechanisms to establish relationships between pronunciations and transcription, we developed a bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) designed to strengthen the connection between audio and text information. BiAM enables the exchange of attention information in both directions, allowing the algorithm to refine its understanding of pronunciation features based on the current text information, and the sequence to be transcribed based on the predicted audio information. Our experimental results on the IEEE Aishubench dataset demonstrate a significant improvement in performance, achieving a 2.5 character error rate reduction compared to the baseline, with even greater benefits observed in noisy conditions.

We introduce and analyze $d_n$ and $\pi_n$, two random processes on the non-negative integers derived from Carre' de Matheron's work, with respect to distance $k_n$. This research extends previous findings by Smilga and Zelenyuk, whose work was limited to cases where $k_n$ remained unchanged or grew at a linear rate, and whose processes converged to the uniform distribution on $\Z_{\geq 0}$. We demonstrate that when $k_n$ remains unchanged or grows linearly, $d_n$ and $\pi_n$ become asymptotically uniformly distributed, whereas for super-linear growth rates, we show $d_n$ and $\pi_n$ approach uniform distributions but at a slower rate. We also introduce $k_n$ dependent generating functions for $d_n$ and $\pi_n$, facilitate the computation of their moments, and establish a relationship with the Bell polynomials.

A detailed study of the critical voltage in superconducting nanowires of varying widths is, both numerically and theoretically, examined by a paper. Using time-dependent $gfmc$ simulations, the critical voltage was determined for a range of widths in a 2d electronic structure. The results show the existence of a voltage-width relationship that can be altered to map voltage as a function of width with applied corrections. The average deviation from this trend is small, and the critical voltage is, precisely, related to the nanowire width. Theoretically, the relativistic NEM dispersion is, successfully, utilized to explain width-dependent behaviors of the critical voltage.

Reconstructing and predicting videos from unseen viewpoints is an intricate task, especially when novel viewpoints are involved. Most current methods either fail to set a clear foundation for understanding or struggle to generalize beyond a limited range of perspectives. In this work, we employ a dual representation consisting of latent images and flow fields to predict videos from novel angles. This approach enables us to generate high-quality novel view predictions without the need for expensive video storage. Furthermore, our method can be generalized to unseen viewpoints and produces implicit constraints that facilitate a more rigorous mathematical analysis. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our network in generating high-resolution high-frame-rate videos from novel perspectives.

We demonstrate a all-wavelength phase beam splitting method using higher-order photonic modes in a highly confined dual-ring photonic system. By leveraging these modes, a 50:50 phase beam splitter is achieved, where the relative phase between combined output waves can be adjusted without changing ring parameters or incident wave positions. This innovation allows for a compact, low-loss device ideal for integrating into photonic circuits needing miniaturized beam combining and splitting components.

Using an effective relativistic three-body chiral dynamics model, this study calculates the mass spectra for $s$-wave $sbb$ baryon resonance states with bottom-quark pairs.  The masses corresponding to different angular momentums are derived from an potential model.  The calculated $s$-wave resonance masses fall within an acceptable range, particularly when accounting for the recently observed $sbb$ baryon resonance state with the symbol $\Xi_{bb}(5810)$.  The resonance masses for $s$-wave $sbb$ baryons are compared with experimentally observed values and theoretical predictions in the literature.  The calculated masses for $s$-wave $sbb$ baryons serve as predictions for future experiments at particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider.  The study does not consider $d$-wave and $g$-wave $sbb$ baryon resonance states.

A mathematical well-mixed model is applied to simulate the distribution of aerosol particles around a person who is infected and producing those particles. The model estimates the concentration of aerosol particles in various scenarios including an infected person in the center of a spherical room, an infected person seated against a wall, and an infected person standing near a wall. The predicted patterns of particle concentration are tested through computational fluid dynamics simulations which consider more complex factors. The study finds that a simplified well-mixed model can provide reasonably accurate predictions even in more intricate environments. The research also highlights key parameters influencing the distribution of aerosol particles including the production rate of particles, the size of the surrounding environment, and the physical characteristics of the infected person. The study provides explicit equations to calculate the distribution of particles in multiple scenarios.

Researchers examined the Nernst effect in highly conductive Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers with numerous Bismuth bands. They discovered that the Nernst coefficient in multi-layered samples behaves like a sum of individual layers' coefficients, but not in a straightforward manner. This is because scattering between different layers complicates the relationship. Nevertheless, reversing the Hall effect current in wide multi-layers can be achieved by injecting a certain level of spin polarization, even though the underlying mechanism is complex.

This study examines the fractional parameter α in an N-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a new $1/r^{2}$ potential, particularly when the potential's coefficient falls within a specific range. We establish the self-adjointness of the corresponding fractional operator and determine its spectrum, showing that it matches the spectrum of the standard Schrödinger equation for certain conditions, while also identifying an additional expression for other scenarios. We provide the complete set of corresponding wave functions.

Recent advances in constraining neural network functions through a bounded $p$-norm likelihood have led to improvements in overfitting control and performance on various tasks, particularly when used in conjunction with network architectures like ResNets and amplitude-aware modules. Reshaping the landscape of a network's loss function via $p$-norm likelihood constraints has demonstrated notable success, yet the impact of this approach on network safety and robustness remains unclear. Furthermore, exploring the effects of $p$-norm likelihood regularization on network safety properties presents a challenging task, given that networks with a constrained gradient norm are not necessarily safer. This study investigates how specifying a network's safety margin through a Lipschitz constant can be achieved without compromising their performance, even as we vary the $p$-norm. A novel approach is proposed that enables exploring a wide range of networks with controlled Lipschitz constants, regardless of their architecture or training method. This approach is comparable to weight decay but yields divergent outcomes, and its implications become more apparent at higher values of $p$. Through various experiments, we provide comprehensive analyses on the trade-offs between a network's safety and performance across different $p$-values, shedding light on novel connections between risk, speech representation flexibility, and note perceivability.

Research into the vector leptoquark D"s_2 has seen progress in searching for its occurrence in top-quark pair productions. To advance this effort, precise predictions for leptoquark pair productions are needed. We present an approach combining permutation invariance and next-to-leading order power-suppressed effects for these productions. Combinations of parton-initised processes yield an enhanced model, which incorporates virtual corrections and allows for meaningful comparisons with other approaches and experimental _data_. Part of this work was supported by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Key Laboratory of Nuclear Physics at Shanghai.

Although deep learning techniques have seen significant progression in low-dose positron emission tomography (PET) denoising research, effective frameworks that incorporate prior knowledge have struggled to achieve notable success. To address this challenge, we present a deep neural network (DNN) framework called DNN-PAD, which combines the benefits of data-driven denoising and prior knowledge exploitation. This framework divides DNN knowledge into two components: a fixed component, consisting of an encoder and a discriminator trained on low-dose PET data, and a trainable component, consisting of a padding network and a generator. By padding the features extracted from low-dose PET images with prior knowledge obtained from MRI and optical PET data, an initial estimation of the denoised image is generated. This prediction is refined through adversarial and convolutional optimization, with the goal of minimizing both perceptual and pixel differences in comparison to the optimal result. Experiments conducted on real patient data demonstrate that the DNN-PAD framework yields superior image quality, as evidenced by lower root mean square error (RMSE) values when compared to currently leading methods.

Neural coreference resolution systems often struggle with consistency, as they may overlook contextual cues and produce conflicting coreference predictions. This study examines whether neural coreference resolution models can effectively capture structural language information, such as that found in centering theory, by integrating domain knowledge through pretraining. The authors developed a novel dataset based on the violation of the nuclearity principle in centering theory and found that using contextualized embeddings can lead to coreference resolution model performance issues, as they fail to generalize well and display increased ambiguity. Furthermore, they introduced a new loss function that improves the performance of models adhering to centering theory constraints. This study provides a valuable framework for assessing neural coreference resolution consistency and explores the potential of knowledge augmentation techniques.

WiFi localization is an established technique with applications in various fields, including navigation systems. However, estimating geospatial distances between WiFi signals in unknown locations remains a challenging task due to signal fluctuations and variations in propagation environments. This study leverages two machine learning techniques, Convolutional Neural Networks and Support Vector Regression, to enhance the accuracy of distance estimation. By utilizing high-resolution spectral features from received signal strength data, our proposed models aim to eliminate varying patterns and simplify signal distributions for more accurate estimation. Experimental results show that both Convolutional Neural Networks and Support Vector Regression offer viable solutions for estimating distances, with improvements in performance exceeding 15% in certain test cases.

When a beam-recycled particle beam interacts with stationary RF fields multiple times within an energy recovery linac (ERL), it can lead to significant beam energy spread due to various effects such as space charge, photon emission, and Compton scattering. A simulation was conducted to examine how different beam patterns affect beam-RF interactions and the resulting beam energy spread during several passes through an ERL. A simple 50 MHz standing wave accelerator was used for this study, with beam pattern simulations showing that the way the beam is arranged can influence the threshold current for acceptable beam energy spread. A pattern known as "head-to-tail" was found to result in increased beam energy spread, while other patterns had varying levels of impact. The effects observed were limited to the immediate beam bunches, and the influence extended no further than 1.5 meters. A more complex accelerator model is necessary to study larger effects over multiple passes.

Researchers examining the double cross effect of two gluons in Quantum Chromodynamics found the findings closely match the amplitudes of six gluons in the N=4 Yang-Mills theory, specifically the most logarithmic components known as the LLX term. This correspondence holds for a scenario where the impact parameter, denoted as b⊥, remains small, and it persists for large transverse momenta (P⊥). The connection between the two theories can be viewed through a lens analogous to the Wigner function, representing the phase-space distribution of color. The small-b⊥ condition, however, presents a contrast to the conventional density evolution of dipole models, yielding an opposite power of gluon density evolution compared to the standard approach. Ultimately, the LLX term's equivalence in both approaches yields the same outcome, despite the differing interpretations of the color factor.

The behavior of polymer brushes curved over a surface is self-adjoint, allowing the calculation of their curvature distributions. Theoretical predictions of thermal fluctuations and stretching forces in curved polymer brushes contradict experimental observations, particularly as they relate to the free energy of stretching, which is unaffected by the sphere's radius in one scenario and follows a distinct pattern in another. To clarify this anomaly, we employ non-affine scaling arguments and Monte Carlo simulations, which validate our hypotheses and reveal the additional influence of local chain conformations on brush behavior. We derive corrections to theoretical predictions by accounting for these non-affine effects, accurately forecasting monomer densities, polymer chain distribution, osmotic pressures, and mean forces in curved brushes.

This paper investigates how cutting off distances beyond a certain threshold λλ(G)=min{λ | d_(·,·) mod λ has a significantly lower dimension, particularly when the graph is modified by cutting off distances greater than λλ). This is shown to be the case for random regular graphs and specific families of expander graphs, with a proof provided for random d-regular graphs with a high probability of occurring, as well as for Cayley graphs of expanders, in contrast to previous findings that only held as the graph size approaches infinity.

An in-depth examination of the luminosity variations in an active galactic nucleus, specifically NGC 4151, was conducted by the Monash UV-Optical Telescopes during the 2000s. Over the course of 11 years, nearly 10,000 observations were collected, mostly at ultraviolet wavelengths, with shorter observation periods also gathered at optical wavelengths. The extensive and diverse dataset posed significant challenges in developing a model capable of capturing the nucleus' long-term variability while accounting for the varying observation parameters. By utilizing statistical techniques, including the comparison of spectral features and changes in scattering light from the host galaxy's bulge, a comprehensive model was created to examine the complex variability patterns of this active galactic nucleus. The resulting analysis revealed the reflection component's contribution to the total variability to be around 20%.
